newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania seeks emergency rule after Vlore battle.
newsitem.headline: Albania seeks emergency rule after Vlore battle.

text.p: Protesters battled riot police in the southern Albanian port of Vlore on Monday and pinned them down in the main police station in anti-government disturbances that left two people dead.

In the capital Tirana, 150 km (90 miles) to the north, Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi blamed the unrest on "terrorist groups" and asked parliament to introduce a state of emergency in the port. Deputies debated the proposal through the evening.

A duty nurse at Vlore hospital said surgeons failed to save the life of a 30-year-old demonstrator shot in the disturbances. The second victim, a man of 51, died of heart failure before reaching hospital.
Up to 100 people were injured, mostly by flying stones, in the clashes which brought to three the number of people killed in two days of trouble.

Protesters drove back police in Vlore's central square where they had gathered peacefully for five days to denounce Berisha and demand the return of savings lost in collapsed pyramid investment schemes.
Protesters punched the air and shouted "Vlore is ours!" Some elderly women cowered and wept in rubble-strewn streets, others trampled captured police shields underfoot.
"We don't want a war, just our money," shouted one young man. "The police are fascists!" shrieked a middle-aged woman.
State television said Meksi asked parliament, dominated by Berisha's supporters, to proclaim emergency rule in Vlore to quell "barbarous acts".

Interior Minister Halit Shamata backed the proposal. He told deputies that the anger of Vlore residents at losing their savings in an investment scheme that collapsed last week "has nothing to do with terrorist and anti-constitutional acts".
But deputies appeared divided on measures curtailing civil liberties and it was not certain the proposal would pass.
Frenzy and hysteria were everywhere in the streets of Vlore as demonstrators pushed police out of the city centre.
About 30 police crouching outside a cafe behind plastic shields were pelted first with stones, then with tables and chairs flung from an overhead terrace.
Some officers surrendered and were ordered to strip off their uniforms, which were thrown onto a bonfire. Others retreated to hills overlooking the town.
Protesters then dragged wrecked cars and oil drums to the police station, erected barricades and set them alight.
Demonstrators and police remained locked in a tense stand-off by the building through most of the day.

One officer who left the station to talk to the crowd, his head heavily bandaged, was chased and badly beaten. By early evening, all protesters had cleared the area around the police station and the city was quiet.
State television showed pictures of the injured in Vlore hospital, some bandaged and dazed, others writhing or lying motionless in beds.

The Health Ministry said 26 people, policemen and protesters, remained in hospital with injuries and 55 were released after treatment. More than 60 policemen were among the injured, including some transferred to a Tirana hospital.
Protesters accuse Berisha's government of failing to warn investors of the pitfalls of pyramid schemes, which have taken in the savings of virtually every family in Albania.
The opposition Forum for Democracy alliance renewed its calls for Berisha to replace his administration with a "technocrat government" to tackle the pyramid crisis.
It called a rally in a Tirana stadium on Wednesday. An opposition demonstration in the capital last weekend, banned by authorities, was broken up by riot police with truncheons.
About 2,000 protesters also gathered in the southern town of Gjirokastra, joined by Albanians working in nearby Greece.

Unrest against the collapse of the schemes first erupted last month in ex-communist Albania, Europe's poorest country. But a rash of arrests and the threat of long jail sentences had kept protesters off streets for a time.
